content.title: Pythagorean Theorem and Distance
content.overview: This lesson covers the relationship between the Pythagorean Theorem and the Distance Formula. You will learn to calculate the straight-line distance between two points on a coordinate plane by treating the horizontal and vertical changes as legs of a right triangle.
learning_objectives: Calculate the horizontal (Δx) and vertical (Δy) changes between two coordinate points.
Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find the distance between two points.
Simplify and approximate square roots to verify distance calculations.

sections.title: The Distance Formula as Geometry
sections.content: The distance between two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is not just a formula to memorize; it is an application of the Pythagorean Theorem (a² + b² = c²). When you connect two points on a grid, you can draw a horizontal line representing the change in x (Δx) and a vertical line representing the change in y (Δy). These two lines form the legs of a right triangle, where the straight-line distance between the points is the hypotenuse.

sections.title: The Delta-Square-Root Strategy
sections.content:
To find the distance, follow these three steps: 1. Find the differences: Δx = x2 − x1 and Δy = y2 − y1. 2. Square and Sum: Calculate (Δx)² + (Δy)². Note that squaring a negative difference always results in a positive number. 3. Square Root: The distance is the positive square root of the sum: d = √[(Δx)² + (Δy)²].

![A flow chart showing the steps: Subtract Coordinates, Square Differences, Sum Squares, Take Square Root.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/16fe3d62-3530-489b-8b5a-9af070fc0c06-1786505971616-321.webp)

sections.title: Simplifying and Approximating
sections.content: ACT answers often appear in exact radical form (e.g., √41) rather than decimals. If the answer choices are decimals, approximate the root by finding the two perfect squares it falls between. For example, since √36 = 6 and √49 = 7, √41 must be approximately 6.4.

worked_examples.question: Points A(−3, 1) and B(2, 5) lie on a coordinate grid. What is the straight-line distance between A and B?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Find the differences. Δx = 2 − (−3) = 5. Δy = 5 − 1 = 4. Step 2: Square and add the differences. 5² + 4² = 25 + 16 = 41. Step 3: Take the square root. The distance is √41. Since 41 is not a perfect square, the exact distance is √41.

common_mistakes: Adding the differences before squaring them.
Forgetting that squaring a negative number (like -3 squared) results in a positive value (9).
Mistakenly adding the coordinates (x1 + x2) instead of subtracting them (x2 - x1).
Choosing a rounded integer (like 7) when the question requires an exact radical (like √41).
exam_tips: If you forget the formula, sketch the points on a grid and draw a right triangle to visualize the legs.
Always check if your final answer is longer than both Δx and Δy; the hypotenuse must be the longest side.
Watch out for coordinates with negative signs; subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive.
content.recap: The distance between two points is the square root of the sum of the squared differences of their coordinates. By treating Δx and Δy as legs of a right triangle, the Pythagorean Theorem provides the straight-line distance.

knowledge_claims.content: The distance between two points on a coordinate plane is the length of the hypotenuse of a right triangle formed by the horizontal and vertical changes.
To find Δx, subtract the x-coordinate of the first point from the x-coordinate of the second point (x2 - x1).
To find Δy, subtract the y-coordinate of the first point from the y-coordinate of the second point (y2 - y1).
When calculating distance, the squares of Δx and Δy are always non-negative, even if the differences themselves are negative.
The Distance Formula is d = √[(x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²].
The value (x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)² represents the square of the distance (d²) according to the Pythagorean Theorem.
The calculated distance must always be greater than or equal to the absolute value of either individual difference (Δx or Δy).
A common error is adding the x and y coordinates together instead of finding the difference between them.
Exact radical form (e.g., √50) is preferred on the ACT unless the answer choices are provided as decimals (e.g., 7.07).
If a point is at (0,0) and another is at (x,y), the distance simplifies to √(x² + y²).
The 'Delta-Square-Root' strategy is triggered whenever a problem asks for the 'straight-line distance' or 'length of a segment' between two coordinate pairs.
To approximate a square root like √41, identify that it sits between √36 (6) and √49 (7).
